name: Bartnik-McKinnon Soliton
description: A static ball of SU(2) Yang-Mills field held together by its own gravity, with a regular centre, no horizon, and flat space far away. Neither a Yang-Mills field nor gravity makes such a ball alone. No formula is known for it: the solutions are found by numerical integration, one for each number of zeros of the field, and every one of them is unstable.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Can a field hold itself together? A Yang-Mills field cannot: the stresses inside a static lump would have to cancel, and a field that pushes outward in every direction cannot arrange that, which was Stanley Deser's argument of 1976 [deser1976, volkov1999]. A year later Sidney Coleman proved that every smooth lump of finite energy radiates its energy away, a theorem he titled "There are no classical glueballs" [coleman1977glueballs]. Gravity by itself has no static lumps either, and when Deser put the two together in three spacetime dimensions, in 1984, they still made nothing static [volkov1999, deser1984eym].¶In four dimensions the answer is yes, and it came from Canberra [bartnik1988]. Robert Bartnik, a research fellow at the Australian National University, and his master's student John McKinnon took a static ball with spherical symmetry and an SU(2) field with only a magnetic part, and integrated the equations on a computer [bartnik1988, oliynyk2025, volkov1999]. They found solutions with no singularity that are flat far away, lumps of nothing but field and curvature, and called them particlelike [bartnik1988]. Gerhard Huisken, a colleague there, remembered "the excitement on the ground floor of the Hanna Neumann building" [oliynyk2025]. Mikhail Volkov and Dmitri Gal'tsov, looking back in their review, called the result "a big surprise" [volkov1999].¶How is such a lump put together? The whole field is one function $w(r)$, equal to $\pm 1$ where there is no field and to $0$ in the field of a magnetic monopole [volkov1999]. Start it at $w = 1$ in the centre, curving away as $1 - br^2/\ell^2$ with $\ell = \sqrt{4\pi G}/(gc^2)$ and $g$ the coupling constant of the field, and for almost every $b$ space closes up on itself in a singularity before any flat end is reached [volkov1999, breitenlohner1994]. At $b = 0.4537$ the function crosses zero once and settles at $w = -1$, and the ball it describes has no horizon and a mass of $0.8286\,c^2\ell/G$ [volkov1999]. Bartnik and McKinnon described it in three layers: a dense core with a sharp edge, a shell where the metric is close to that of a charged black hole around a magnetic monopole, and a far region close to Schwarzschild's [bartnik1988].¶The balance holds only on a ladder: there is one soliton for each number $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ of zeros of $w$, with masses $0.8286$, $0.9713$, $0.9953$, and onward toward $1$ in the same units [volkov1999]. Each further zero pinches the ball tighter at $r = \ell$, and Peter Breitenlohner, Peter Forgács, and Dieter Maison followed the ladder to its end, where the outside of the ball is the extreme Reissner-Nordström black hole of a magnetic monopole [breitenlohner1994, volkov1999]. No formula is known for any rung, and even the existence of the first as a smooth solution was proved only in 1991, by Joel Smoller, Arthur Wasserman, Shing-Tung Yau, and J. B. McLeod [volkov1999, smoller1991, breitenlohner1994]. The proof for the whole ladder followed from Smoller and Wasserman two years later [smoller1993]. A horizon can sit in the middle as well: in 1989 and 1990 Volkov and Gal'tsov, H. P. Künzle and A. K. M. Masood-ul-Alam, and Piotr Bizoń found black holes dressed in the same field, which the conjecture that a black hole has no hair had ruled out [volkov1989, kunzle1990, bizon1990, volkov1999]. The balls need not be round either: Burkhard Kleihaus and Jutta Kunz found static ones with only an axis of symmetry, and wrote the round ones in isotropic coordinates on the way [kleihaus1998].¶The ball does not last: Norbert Straumann and Zhi-Hong Zhou found one radial perturbation of the first soliton that grows exponentially [straumann1990]. When Zhou and Straumann followed the perturbation as it grew, the soliton either collapsed to a Schwarzschild black hole or exploded [zhou1991]. The reason came from Gal'tsov and Volkov in 1991: the soliton sits on top of the energy barrier between two vacua of the Yang-Mills field, where the sphaleron of the electroweak theory sits [galtsov1991, volkov1999]. George Lavrelashvili and Dieter Maison counted $2n$ unstable modes for the $n$th soliton, $n$ of each parity [lavrelashvili1995, volkov1999].¶An unstable soliton still has a use, which Matthew Choptuik, Tadeusz Chmaj, and Bizoń found in 1996 when they sent pulses of Yang-Mills field inward on a computer and tuned them to the edge between dispersing and making a black hole [choptuik1996]. For some families of pulses the field at the edge settled onto the first soliton, and the closer the tuning the longer it stayed, by the logarithm of the distance from the edge [choptuik1996]. The smallest black hole such a family makes has the soliton's mass to within a percent [choptuik1996]. Why the balance exists was still unexplained when Volkov and Gal'tsov wrote their review: it "still does not find a clear explanation in physical terms" [volkov1999].

related.text: The solitons' outside in the limit of infinitely many zeros. As $n \to \infty$ the metric beyond $r = \ell$ tends to the extreme Reissner-Nordström black hole of a magnetic monopole, $1 - 2m/r \to (1 - \ell/r)^2$ [breitenlohner1994, volkov1999].

The solitons' edge in the same limit. As $n \to \infty$ the sphere $r = \ell$ recedes to an infinite distance from the centre, and the metric near it tends to the product of a pseudosphere and a sphere of radius $\ell$ [breitenlohner1994].

The other ball of field held together by its own gravity and known only numerically, made of a massive scalar field with a turning phase. Boson stars up to the heaviest are stable, and every one of these solitons is unstable [gleiser1989, lee1989, volkov1999].

The static sphere with both of its functions free, $e^{2\Phi} = \sigma^2(1 - 2m/r)$. A star fills it with fluid; the soliton fills it with a Yang-Mills field, whose stress along the radius differs from its stress across it.

The soliton's far field, and one of its two fates. Far from the centre the metric approaches Schwarzschild's of the soliton's mass, and a perturbed soliton either collapses to a Schwarzschild black hole or explodes [bartnik1988, zhou1991].
Another static ball with no surface, whose stress along the radius differs from its stress across it. Einstein made his of particles on circular orbits, and it can be written in closed form.

Collapse at the threshold, with a scalar field. Roberts's solution looks the same at every scale, as the critical solution does on one of the two thresholds Choptuik, Chmaj, and Bizoń found for a Yang-Mills field; on the other the critical solution is the first soliton [choptuik1996].

parameters.description: Lapse function, dimensionless: a clock held at radius $r$ runs at $\sigma\sqrt{1 - 2m/r}$ of the rate $t$ counts. On a solution $\partial_r\sigma = 2\ell^2\sigma\left(\partial_r w\right)^2/r$, and $\sigma \to 1$ far away fixes the constant it would otherwise carry

Mass function, a length: $m = GM(r)/c^2$ with $M(r)$ the mass inside the sphere of radius $r$, and $m(0) = 0$. On a solution $\partial_r m = \ell^2\left(1 - 2m/r\right)\left(\partial_r w\right)^2 + \ell^2\left(1 - w^2\right)^2/(2r^2)$, the energy of the Yang-Mills field in each shell

Amplitude of the Yang-Mills field, dimensionless: the SU(2) potential is purely magnetic, with $w = \pm 1$ where there is no field and $w = 0$ in the field of a magnetic monopole. On a solution $r^2\left(1 - 2m/r\right)\partial_r^2 w + \left(2m - \ell^2\left(1 - w^2\right)^2/r\right)\partial_r w + w\left(1 - w^2\right) = 0$. A solution regular at the centre and flat far away exists for one starting value $b$ in $w = 1 - br^2/\ell^2 + \dots$ for each number $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ of zeros of $w$, and is known only numerically

The one length of the theory, $\ell = \sqrt{4\pi G}/(gc^2)$ with $g$ the coupling constant of the Yang-Mills field, so that masses come in units of $c^2\ell/G$. The soliton with one zero has $b = 0.4537$ and the mass $0.8286\,c^2\ell/G$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The mass function $m(r)$ and the unit $\ell$ are lengths, the lapse function $\sigma(r)$ and the amplitude $w(r)$ of the Yang-Mills field are dimensionless, and we leave the three functions free, since no solution is known in closed form. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Tortoise

parameters.description: Dimensionless, the factor that multiplies the flat plane of $t$ and $\xi$: a clock held at $\xi$ runs at $\sqrt{F}$ of the rate $t$ counts, and $F \to 1$ far away. In the functions of the areal radius it is $\sigma^2 N$ on the same sphere
Areal radius of the sphere at $\xi$, a length, with $r(0) = 0$ and $\partial_\xi r = \sigma N$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \xi, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\xi$ the tortoise coordinate, a length measured from the centre, with $d\xi/dr = 1/(\sigma N)$ for the areal radius $r$, the lapse function $\sigma$, and $N = 1 - 2m/r$ with $m$ the mass function. The function $F(\xi)$ is dimensionless, $r(\xi)$ is a length, and we leave both free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
